maria-rundell.name: Maria Rundell
maria-rundell.summary: English writer who, unpaid, sent an unedited recipe collection to publisher John Murray in her sixties; the resulting 1805 cookbook became a huge bestseller aimed at middle-class housewives.

a-new-system-of-domestic-cookery.name: A New System of Domestic Cookery
a-new-system-of-domestic-cookery.summary: An 1806 cookery book by Maria Rundell that became the most popular English cookbook of the early 19th century, running to over 67 editions.
a-new-system-of-domestic-cookery.source_title: A New System of Domestic Cookery

joseph-fry-type-founder.name: Joseph Fry
joseph-fry-type-founder.summary: English type-founder and chocolate maker (1728–1787) who founded the family firm that became J. S. Fry & Sons.

auguste-escoffier.name: Auguste Escoffier
auguste-escoffier.summary: French chef (1846–1935) who modernised French cooking, codified the five mother sauces, and created the kitchen brigade system still used today.

le-guide-culinaire.name: Le Guide Culinaire
le-guide-culinaire.summary: Georges Auguste Escoffier's 1903 cookbook of French restaurant cuisine, developed while he worked at the Savoy, Ritz and Carlton hotels; still in print.

les-halles.name: Les Halles
les-halles.summary: Paris's former central fresh food market, which operated until 1973 and was later replaced, first by an unpopular shopping centre and then by the modern Westfield Forum des Halles mall.

eliza-acton.name: Eliza Acton
eliza-acton.summary: English food writer who published one of Britain's first cookery books for home cooks, Modern Cookery for Private Families, in 1845.

modern-cookery-for-private-families.name: Modern Cookery for Private Families
modern-cookery-for-private-families.summary: An 1845 English cookbook by Eliza Acton, a bestseller through 13 editions by 1853, praised for pioneering precise ingredient lists, quantities and cooking times.

bee-wilson.name: Bee Wilson
bee-wilson.summary: British food writer and journalist known for a Wall Street Journal column and for campaigning for food education through the charity TastEd.

service-la-russe.name: Service à la russe
service-la-russe.summary: A style of serving meals course by course to each guest individually, developed in France in the 19th century from Russian table customs, which gradually replaced service à la française.

urbain-dubois.name: Urbain Dubois
urbain-dubois.summary: A French chef (1818–1901) known for classic French recipe books, for creating Veal Orloff, and for popularizing service à la russe in Western European dining.

hindoostane-coffee-house.name: Hindoostane Coffee House
hindoostane-coffee-house.summary: The first Indian restaurant in the British Isles, opened in London in 1810 by Sake Dean Mahomed and closed in 1833 after he went bankrupt.

dean-mahomed.name: Dean Mahomed
dean-mahomed.summary: British Indian traveller, soldier, surgeon and entrepreneur (1759-1851) who introduced Indian cuisine and shampoo baths to Europe and was one of the earliest notable non-European immigrants to the West.

the-epicure-s-almanack.name: The Epicure's Almanack
the-epicure-s-almanack.summary: 1815 guide to eating establishments in London, written by Ralph Rylance; poorly received at first but republished by the British Library in 2013.

marie-antoine-car-me.name: Marie-Antoine Carême
marie-antoine-car-me.summary: French chef who pioneered elaborate 'grande cuisine' for the elite, cooked for figures such as Talleyrand and Tsar Alexander I, and wrote influential books that codified classical French cookery.

john-constable.name: John Constable
john-constable.summary: English Romantic landscape painter (1776–1837) known for scenes of Dedham Vale, though he was never financially successful in his own country.

j-m-w-turner.name: J. M. W. Turner
j-m-w-turner.summary: English Romantic painter (1775–1851) admired for his light, atmosphere, and bold colour, whose work inspired impressionists like Monet; a child prodigy elected to the Royal Academy at 27.

walter-benjamin.name: Walter Benjamin
walter-benjamin.summary: German philosopher, cultural critic and essayist (1892–1940) associated with the Frankfurt School, often seen in popular culture and left-wing journalism as an exemplar of the tragedy of German Jewish intellectuals under Nazi Germany.

jean-auguste-dominique-ingres.name: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
jean-auguste-dominique-ingres.summary: A French Neoclassical painter (1780–1867) known especially for his portraits, who upheld academic tradition against Romanticism yet influenced later modernists like Matisse and Picasso.

eug-ne-delacroix.name: Eugène Delacroix
eug-ne-delacroix.summary: A French Romantic painter (1798–1863) regarded as leader of the French Romantic school, favoring colour and movement over the clarity of outline preferred by his rival Ingres.

orientalism.name: Orientalism
orientalism.summary: The depiction of the Eastern world by Western artists and writers, later reinterpreted since Edward Said's 1978 book as a patronizing Western attitude toward Asian and North African societies.

claude-monet.name: Claude Monet
claude-monet.summary: French painter (1840–1926) and founder of Impressionism, known for outdoor landscape paintings capturing his perceptions of light and nature.

oxford-movement.name: Oxford Movement
oxford-movement.summary: A high-church movement within the Church of England, begun in the 1830s at Oxford, that revived older Christian traditions and developed into Anglo-Catholicism; many participants later became Catholic.

gothic-revival-architecture.name: Gothic Revival architecture
gothic-revival-architecture.summary: An architectural movement reviving medieval Gothic styles, becoming widespread in the first half of the 19th century and dominant in the West until the 1880s.

high-victorian-gothic.name: High Victorian Gothic
high-victorian-gothic.summary: A mid-to-late 19th-century architectural style, a branch of the Gothic Revival promoted by John Ruskin and known for multicoloured, textured Gothic decoration.

charles-barry.name: Sir Charles Barry
charles-barry.summary: English architect (1795-1860) best known for rebuilding the Palace of Westminster and for popularising Italianate architecture in Britain.

augustus-pugin.name: Augustus Pugin
augustus-pugin.summary: English architect (1812–1852) who pioneered the Gothic Revival style and designed the interior and clock tower of the Palace of Westminster.

george-gilbert-scott.name: George Gilbert Scott
george-gilbert-scott.summary: English Gothic Revival architect (1811–1878) who designed or altered over 800 buildings, including London's Albert Memorial and the St Pancras station hotel.

william-butterfield.name: William Butterfield
william-butterfield.summary: British Gothic Revival architect (1814–1900) associated with the Oxford Movement, known for his use of polychromy.

albert-memorial.name: Albert Memorial
albert-memorial.summary: Gothic Revival memorial in Kensington Gardens, London, commissioned by Queen Victoria in memory of Prince Albert and completed in the 1870s by Sir George Gilbert Scott.

greek-revival-architecture.name: Greek Revival architecture
greek-revival-architecture.summary: An architectural style reviving forms of ancient Greek temples, flourishing in the late 18th and early 19th centuries across northern Europe, the United States and newly independent Greece.

william-wilkins-architect.name: William Wilkins
william-wilkins-architect.summary: English architect and classical scholar (1778–1839) who designed London's National Gallery, University College London, and Downing College, Cambridge.

downing-college-cambridge.name: Downing College
downing-college-cambridge.summary: A Cambridge University college founded in 1800, the only one added to the university between 1596 and 1869, known for law and medicine.

robert-smirke-architect.name: Robert Smirke
robert-smirke-architect.summary: English architect (1780–1867) and a leader of Greek Revival style who designed the British Museum's main block and façade, pioneering structural iron and concrete foundations.

douard-manet.name: Édouard Manet
douard-manet.summary: French painter (1832–1883) who bridged Realism and Impressionism; his controversial works Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe and Olympia are seen as marking the start of modern art.

haussmann-s-renovation-of-paris.name: Haussmannization
haussmann-s-renovation-of-paris.summary: The vast 1853–1870 rebuilding of Paris commissioned by Napoleon III and directed by Georges-Eugène Haussmann, clearing crowded medieval districts for wide avenues and new infrastructure.

john-linnell-painter.name: John Linnell
john-linnell-painter.summary: English engraver, portrait and landscape painter, a naturalist and rival of John Constable, with a taste for Northern European Renaissance art and ties to William Blake's circle.

paul-sandby.name: Paul Sandby
paul-sandby.summary: English mapmaker and landscape painter (1731–1809), a founding member of the Royal Academy in 1768.

thomas-girtin.name: Thomas Girtin
thomas-girtin.summary: An English watercolourist and etcher (1775–1802), a friend and rival of J. M. W. Turner who helped establish watercolour as a respected art form.

king-s-library.name: King's Library
king-s-library.summary: A vast Enlightenment-era book collection assembled by Britain's King George III, over 65,000 volumes given to the nation by George IV and long housed in a purpose-built British Museum gallery.

montagu-house-bloomsbury.name: Montagu House
montagu-house-bloomsbury.summary: A 17th-century London mansion that became the first home of the British Museum in 1759, before being demolished in the 1840s.

british-museum-reading-room.name: Round Reading Room
british-museum-reading-room.summary: Circular reading room at the centre of the British Museum, designed by Sydney Smirke and opened in 1857, formerly the main reading room of the British Library.

john-crome.name: John Crome
john-crome.summary: English landscape painter (1768–1821), a founding member of the Norwich School who spent his life in Norwich painting Norfolk scenes.

john-sell-cotman.name: John Sell Cotman
john-sell-cotman.summary: English landscape painter and etcher (1782–1842), a leading member of the Norwich School, Britain's first provincial art movement.

james-stark-painter.name: James Stark
james-stark-painter.summary: English landscape painter (1794–1859), a leading member of the Norwich School who trained under John Crome and became its president in 1829.

joseph-stannard.name: Joseph Stannard
joseph-stannard.summary: English marine, landscape and portrait painter (1797–1830), a prominent member of the Norwich School of painters.

thomas-davidson-painter.name: Thomas Davidson
thomas-davidson-painter.summary: An English painter (1842–1919) who specialized in historical naval scenes.

horatio-nelson-1st-viscount-nelson.name: Horatio Nelson
horatio-nelson-1st-viscount-nelson.summary: British Royal Navy officer (1758 to 1805) whose leadership and tactics won decisive naval victories in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, regarded as one of history's greatest admirals.

george-arnald.name: George Arnald
george-arnald.summary: British painter (1763–1841) who specialised in landscapes and topographical views, best known for his celebrated painting of the Battle of the Nile.

lemuel-francis-abbott.name: Lemuel Francis Abbott
lemuel-francis-abbott.summary: An English portrait painter (1760/61–1803) best known for his portrait of Horatio Nelson and other naval and literary figures of the era.

thomas-hamilton-architect.name: Thomas Hamilton
thomas-hamilton-architect.summary: A Scottish architect (1784–1858) based in Edinburgh, a leading Greek Revivalist known for buildings including the Burns Monument and the Royal High School.

hugh-william-williams.name: Hugh William Williams
hugh-william-williams.summary: Scottish landscape painter (1773–1829), known as 'Grecian Williams.'

royal-high-school-edinburgh.name: Royal High School, Edinburgh
royal-high-school-edinburgh.summary: A co-educational school in Edinburgh founded in 1128, one of the oldest schools in Scotland, serving around 1,400 pupils today.

otto-von-bismarck.name: Otto von Bismarck
otto-von-bismarck.summary: German statesman (1815–1898) who oversaw the unification of Germany through three wars and served as its first chancellor from 1871 to 1890, known as the "Iron Chancellor."

napoleon-iii.name: Napoleon III
napoleon-iii.summary: Nephew of Napoleon I, first elected President of France (1848–1852) then Emperor of the French until 1870, when he was captured by Prussia and its allies at the Battle of Sedan.

battle-of-sedan.name: Battle of Sedan
battle-of-sedan.summary: A battle fought on 1 to 2 September 1870 in the Franco-Prussian War, in which Prussian and allied forces encircled and captured Emperor Napoleon III with over 100,000 French troops, deciding the war for Prussia.

wilhelm-i.name: Wilhelm I
wilhelm-i.summary: King of Prussia from 1861 and the first German Emperor, from 1871 until his death in 1888, as head of the newly united Germany.

alsace.name: Alsace
alsace.summary: Cultural region in northeastern France on the Rhine, with a blend of German and French influences, ceded to Germany after the Franco-Prussian War in 1871.

lorraine.name: Lorraine
lorraine.summary: A historical region of eastern France, ceded to Germany along with Alsace after the Franco-Prussian War.

am-d-e-courbet.name: Amédée Courbet
am-d-e-courbet.summary: French admiral (1827–1885) who won major land and naval victories in the Tonkin Campaign and the Sino-French War of 1884–85.

sino-french-war.name: Sino-French War
sino-french-war.summary: An 1884–85 conflict between France and the Qing dynasty over influence in Vietnam, which ended with China ceding Vietnam as French protectorates.

fuzhou.name: Fuzhou
fuzhou.summary: The capital of China's Fujian province, historically known in the West as Foochow, and now a major city of over 8 million people.

tonkin.name: Tonkin
tonkin.summary: A historical name for the Red River Delta region of northern Vietnam, later used for the French colonial protectorate there from 1883 to 1945.

satsuma-rebellion.name: Satsuma Rebellion
satsuma-rebellion.summary: An 1877 revolt of disaffected samurai against Japan's new Meiji government, crushed after nine months; it ended the samurai class and ushered in a conscript-based modern army.

saig-takamori.name: Saigō Takamori
saig-takamori.summary: A Japanese samurai and politician (1828-1877) who helped overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate in 1868, then led the failed Satsuma Rebellion against the new Meiji government in 1877, dying in the fighting.

shogun.name: Shogun
shogun.summary: Title of Japan's military rulers from 1185 to 1868, who governed through the bakufu (their military government) while nominally appointed by the Emperor.

jules-brunet.name: Jules Brunet
jules-brunet.summary: A French military officer (1838–1911) who trained the Tokugawa shogunate's army, then fought alongside the rebel Republic of Ezo in Japan's Boshin War before returning to serve in the Franco-Prussian War.

louis-mile-bertin.name: Bertin
louis-mile-bertin.summary: French naval engineer (1840–1924), one of the foremost of his time, who championed fast, powerfully armed light warships over large battleships.

lake-poets.name: Lake Poets
lake-poets.summary: A group of English Romantic poets, chiefly Wordsworth, Coleridge and Southey, who lived in England's Lake District in the early 19th century; the name was first used to mock them.

william-wordsworth.name: William Wordsworth
william-wordsworth.summary: English Romantic poet (1770–1850) who, with Coleridge, helped launch the Romantic Age in English literature through their 1798 Lyrical Ballads.

samuel-taylor-coleridge.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
samuel-taylor-coleridge.summary: English poet, critic and philosopher (1772–1834), a founder of the Romantic Movement, best known for The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

robert-southey.name: Robert Southey
robert-southey.summary: English Romantic poet (1774–1843) and Poet Laureate from 1813 until his death, remembered for "After Blenheim" and the original "Goldilocks and the Three Bears".

walter-scott.name: Walter Scott
walter-scott.summary: A Scottish novelist, poet and historian (1771–1832), famed for his Waverley novels and narrative poems such as Marmion, credited with establishing the historical novel as a genre.

charles-dickens.name: Charles Dickens
charles-dickens.summary: English writer and journalist (1812–1870) regarded by many as the greatest novelist of the Victorian era, famed for creating some of literature's best-known characters.

victor-hugo.name: Victor Hugo
victor-hugo.summary: French Romantic writer (1802–1885) best known for the novels The Hunchback of Notre-Dame and Les Misérables, who also campaigned against slavery and capital punishment.

prosper-m-rim-e.name: Prosper Mérimée
prosper-m-rim-e.summary: A French Romantic writer (1803 to 1870) and pioneer of the novella, best known for Carmen; as inspector of French historical monuments he oversaw preservation of sites like Notre-Dame de Paris.

william-le-queux.name: William Le Queux
william-le-queux.summary: French-English journalist and writer (1864–1927) best known for invasion-fantasy novels, including The Great War in England in 1897 and the bestselling The Invasion of 1910.

the-great-war-in-england-in-1897.name: The Great War in England in 1897
the-great-war-in-england-in-1897.summary: An 1894 invasion novel by William Le Queux, first serialised in the magazine Answers and later published as a book that ran to eight editions.
the-great-war-in-england-in-1897.source_title: The Great War in England in 1897

the-lay-of-the-last-minstrel.name: The Lay of the Last Minstrel
the-lay-of-the-last-minstrel.summary: An 1805 narrative poem in six cantos by Walter Scott, set in the Scottish Borders in the mid-16th century and framed as sung by a minstrel.
the-lay-of-the-last-minstrel.source_title: The Lay of the Last Minstrel

marmion-poem.name: Marmion
marmion-poem.summary: 1808 historical romance in verse by Sir Walter Scott, set in 16th-century Scotland and England and ending with the 1513 Battle of Flodden.

robert-browning.name: Robert Browning
robert-browning.summary: English poet and playwright (1812-1889) known for dramatic monologues; married fellow poet Elizabeth Barrett in 1846 and became a leading Victorian literary figure, notably with The Ring and the Book.

the-ring-and-the-book.name: The Ring and the Book
the-ring-and-the-book.summary: 21,000-line dramatic narrative poem by Robert Browning, published in four volumes from 1868 to 1869, showcasing his dramatic-monologue style.

elizabeth-barrett-browning.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
elizabeth-barrett-browning.summary: English Victorian poet, popular in her lifetime, who campaigned against slavery and married fellow poet Robert Browning after her 1844 success Poems.

sonnets-from-the-portuguese.name: Sonnets from the Portuguese
sonnets-from-the-portuguese.summary: A collection of 44 love sonnets by Elizabeth Barrett Browning, written around 1845–46 and published in 1850, despite its title entirely her own work.

aurora-leigh.name: Aurora Leigh
aurora-leigh.summary: An 1856 verse novel by Elizabeth Barrett Browning, narrated by its heroine and regarded as a major work of Victorian poetry and feminist literature.

fran-ois-ren-de-chateaubriand.name: François-René de Chateaubriand
fran-ois-ren-de-chateaubriand.summary: French writer, politician and diplomat (1768–1848) who influenced 19th-century French literature, defended the Catholic faith in Génie du christianisme, and served as foreign minister.

the-genius-of-christianity.name: The Genius of Christianity
the-genius-of-christianity.summary: Work by François-René de Chateaubriand defending Christianity against Enlightenment and revolutionary attacks, published in 1802; a major inspiration for the Romantic movement in art and literature.

napoleon.name: Napoleon
napoleon.summary: French emperor from 1804 to 1814, and briefly in 1815, who rose to power as a general during the French Revolution and led sweeping military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East.

stendhal.name: Stendhal
stendhal.summary: Pen name of French writer Marie-Henri Beyle (1783–1842), author of The Red and the Black and The Charterhouse of Parma, regarded as an early master of psychological realism.

george-sand.name: George Sand
george-sand.summary: Pen name of French novelist Amantine Dupin (1804–1876), a leading figure of European Romanticism who advocated for women's rights and criticized marriage.

condition-of-england-question.name: Condition-of-England question
condition-of-england-question.summary: A Victorian-era debate over the English working class during the Industrial Revolution, first raised by Thomas Carlyle in his 1839 essay Chartism.

thomas-carlyle.name: Thomas Carlyle
thomas-carlyle.summary: A Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher (1795–1881), known as the 'sage of Chelsea,' whose writings, including The French Revolution: A History, strongly shaped Victorian intellectual culture.

the-battle-of-dorking.name: The Battle of Dorking
the-battle-of-dorking.summary: An 1871 novella by George Chesney depicting a German-speaking power invading Britain, credited with starting the invasion-literature genre.

george-chesney.name: George Chesney
george-chesney.summary: British Army officer, politician and writer (1830–1895), remembered as the author of the 1871 novella The Battle of Dorking, a founding work of invasion literature.

dante-gabriel-rossetti.name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
dante-gabriel-rossetti.summary: English poet and painter (1828–1882) who founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848 and later influenced Symbolist and Aesthetic art.

pre-raphaelite-brotherhood.name: Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
pre-raphaelite-brotherhood.summary: A group of English painters, poets and critics founded in 1848 who sought a return to the detail and colour of early Italian art and rejected the influence of Raphael and the Royal Academy.

christina-rossetti.name: Christina Rossetti
christina-rossetti.summary: English poet (1830–1894) known for romantic and devotional verse, including 'Goblin Market,' and for Christmas carols still sung in Britain.

paul-verlaine.name: Paul Verlaine
paul-verlaine.summary: French poet (1844–1896) associated with the Symbolist, Parnassianist and Decadent movements, known for his tempestuous relationship with fellow poet Arthur Rimbaud.

po-te-maudit.name: Poète maudit
po-te-maudit.summary: A French term for a poet living outside or against society, whose life is often marked by insanity, crime, addiction or an early death; applied to poets like Rimbaud and Mallarmé.

st-phane-mallarm.name: Stéphane Mallarmé
st-phane-mallarm.summary: French poet and critic (1842 to 1898), a major Symbolist figure whose work influenced Cubism, Futurism, Dadaism, and Surrealism.

arthur-rimbaud.name: Arthur Rimbaud
arthur-rimbaud.summary: A French poet (1854–1891) known for surreal, transgressive themes and lasting influence on modern literature, including the work A Season in Hell.

jean-mor-as.name: Jean Moréas
jean-mor-as.summary: A Greek-born poet, essayist and art critic (1856–1910), born Ioannis Papadiamantopoulos, who wrote mostly in French.

panjdeh-incident.name: Panjdeh Incident
panjdeh-incident.summary: An 1885 armed clash between Russia and Afghanistan over a border fort that triggered a diplomatic crisis with Britain, halting Russian expansion in Central Asia and fixing Afghanistan's northwest border.

fashoda-incident.name: Fashoda Incident
fashoda-incident.summary: A 1898 crisis between Britain and France over control of the Upper Nile in Sudan, which brought both empires to the brink of war before France withdrew.

edinburgh-review.name: Edinburgh Review
edinburgh-review.summary: A series of British intellectual and cultural magazines; the best-known and longest-running version was published from 1802 to 1929.

entente-cordiale.name: Entente Cordiale
entente-cordiale.summary: Series of agreements signed on 8 April 1904 between the United Kingdom and France that significantly improved Anglo-French relations.

the-invasion-of-1910.name: The Invasion of 1910
the-invasion-of-1910.summary: An 1906 invasion-literature novel mainly by William Le Queux depicting a German occupation of Britain, viewed as both Germanophobic and prescient about coming war.

london-smallpox-hospital.name: London Smallpox Hospital
london-smallpox-hospital.summary: A hospital established in London in 1745–6, said to be the first of its kind in Europe, dedicated to treating smallpox patients.

liverpool-and-manchester-railway.name: Liverpool and Manchester Railway
liverpool-and-manchester-railway.summary: The world's first inter-city railway, opening in 1830 between Liverpool and Manchester, the first to use only steam locomotives, run double track throughout, and be fully timetabled.

metropolitan-asylums-board.name: Metropolitan Asylums Board
metropolitan-asylums-board.summary: A body established in 1867 under London's Poor Law to care for the city's sick and poor, building hospitals such as those for smallpox, until it was dissolved in 1930.

planet-locomotive.name: Planet
planet-locomotive.summary: An early steam locomotive built in 1830 by Robert Stephenson and Company for the Liverpool and Manchester Railway.

henri-poincar.name: Henri Poincaré
henri-poincar.summary: French mathematician, theoretical physicist, engineer, and philosopher of science (1854–1912), often called a polymath and "The Last Universalist" for excelling across every field of mathematics in his lifetime.

louis-couturat.name: Louis Couturat
louis-couturat.summary: A French logician, mathematician, philosopher and linguist (1868–1914), a pioneer of the constructed language Ido.

science-and-hypothesis.name: Science and Hypothesis
science-and-hypothesis.summary: 1902 book by mathematician Henri Poincaré arguing that scientific truths are convenient conventions rather than absolute certainties; it influenced Einstein's 1905 papers.

hms-atlas-1860.name: HMS Atlas
hms-atlas-1860.summary: A 91-gun Royal Navy ship launched in 1860 that was never completed for combat and instead served in reserve and as a hospital ship until 1904.

hms-endymion-1865.name: HMS Endymion
hms-endymion-1865.summary: A 21-gun Royal Navy wooden frigate commissioned in 1866, later used from 1881 as a hospital ship for the Metropolitan Asylums Board.

gravesend.name: Gravesend
gravesend.summary: A town in northwest Kent, England, on the south bank of the River Thames, with a population of about 60,250 in 2021 and a long maritime history.

hulme.name: Hulme
hulme.summary: An inner-city area of Manchester, England, just south of the city centre, with a significant industrial heritage; its name derives from an Old Norse word for a small island or marshy land.

acts-of-union-1800.name: Act of Union 1800
acts-of-union-1800.summary: Legislation merging the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland into the United Kingdom, effective from January 1801; still partly in force in the UK.

united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-irel.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-irel.summary: The state formed in 1801 by uniting the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland, lasting until 1922 when the Irish Free State gained independence.
united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-irel.source_title: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

napoleon-ii.name: Napoleon II
napoleon-ii.summary: Son of Napoleon I, disputed as Emperor of the French for two weeks in 1815 as a boy; he never actually ruled and died of tuberculosis in Vienna at 21.

cape-colony.name: Cape Colony
cape-colony.summary: A colony in what is now South Africa, held by the Dutch from 1652 and then, from 1795-1802 and 1806-1910, by Britain, before it joined with three others to form the Union of South Africa.

great-trek.name: Great Trek
great-trek.summary: A northward migration from 1836 onward of Dutch-speaking Boer settlers leaving Cape Colony to escape British rule, leading to the founding of several Boer republics.

nguy-n-dynasty.name: Nguyễn dynasty
nguy-n-dynasty.summary: The last Vietnamese dynasty, ruling unified Vietnam from 1802 until the French protectorate began in 1883, and nominally until 1945 when the last emperor abolished the treaty with France.

cochinchina-campaign.name: Cochinchina campaign
cochinchina-campaign.summary: A series of French and Spanish military operations from 1858 to 1862 against Vietnam that opened the French conquest of Vietnam and led to the colony of Cochinchina.

treaty-of-saigon-1862.name: Treaty of Saigon (1862)
treaty-of-saigon-1862.summary: 1862 treaty in which Emperor Tự Đức of the Nguyễn dynasty ceded Saigon and three southern Vietnamese provinces to France and Spain.

cochinchina.name: Cochinchina
cochinchina.summary: Historical name for southern Vietnam, originally the Đàng Trong domain of the Nguyễn lords in the 17th-18th centuries, later a French colony from the 1860s.

french-indochina.name: French Indochina
french-indochina.summary: A federation of French-ruled territories in Southeast Asia, including Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, that existed from 1887 to 1954, with capitals at Hanoi and Saigon.

slavery-abolition-act-1833.name: Slavery Abolition Act 1833
slavery-abolition-act-1833.summary: An 1833 British law that abolished slavery across most of the empire through compensated emancipation, freeing about 800,000 people.

orange-free-state.name: Orange Free State
orange-free-state.summary: Landlocked Boer republic in southern Africa between the Orange and Vaal rivers, independent from 1854 until its defeat by Britain ended it in the Second Boer War of 1902.

south-african-republic.name: South African Republic
south-african-republic.summary: A landlocked Boer republic, also called the Transvaal Republic, existing from 1852 to 1902, when it was annexed by Britain after the Second Boer War.

second-boer-war.name: Second Boer War
second-boer-war.summary: A war from 1899 to 1902 between the British Empire and the Boer republics over British influence in Southern Africa, ending in British annexation of both republics.

treaty-of-hu-1883.name: Treaty of Huế (1883)
treaty-of-hu-1883.summary: Also known as the Harmand Treaty, it was dictated by French administrator François-Jules Harmand after France seized the Thuận An forts in August 1883.

annam-french-protectorate.name: Annam
annam-french-protectorate.summary: A French protectorate covering central Vietnam from 1883 to 1949, nominally ruled by the Vietnamese Nguyễn dynasty and later folded into French Indochina.

treaty-of-hu-1884.name: Treaty of Huế (1884)
treaty-of-hu-1884.summary: Also called the Patenôtre Treaty, it was negotiated by Jules Patenôtre and formed the basis of French colonial rule in Vietnam for seven decades, until the 1949 Élysée Accords.

cheap-trains-act-1883.name: Cheap Trains Act 1883
cheap-trains-act-1883.summary: An 1883 UK act that removed passenger duty on cheap train fares and required railway companies to run more low-cost trains for workers.

treaty-of-tianjin-1885.name: Treaty of Tianjin (1885)
treaty-of-tianjin-1885.summary: 1885 treaty ending the Sino-French War, forcing China to recognize France's protectorate over Annam and Tonkin and abandon its claims over Vietnam.

john-stuart-mill.name: John Stuart Mill
john-stuart-mill.summary: English philosopher and politician (1806–1873), a leading liberal thinker who championed individual liberty, women's rights and utilitarianism, author of On Liberty.

on-liberty.name: On Liberty
on-liberty.summary: 1859 essay by Harriet Taylor Mill and John Stuart Mill applying utilitarianism to the relationship between individual liberty and state authority, warning against the 'tyranny of the majority.'

jeremy-bentham.name: Jeremy Bentham
jeremy-bentham.summary: An English philosopher and jurist (1748–1832) regarded as the founder of modern utilitarianism, who argued for the greatest happiness of the greatest number and advocated abolishing slavery and capital punishment.

auguste-comte.name: Auguste Comte
auguste-comte.summary: French philosopher (1798–1857) who coined the term sociology and founded the doctrine of positivism, influencing thinkers such as John Stuart Mill.

george-boole.name: George Boole
george-boole.summary: English mathematician and philosopher (1815–1864) who transformed logic into a mathematical, algebraic system using binary values, later becoming Queen's College Cork's first professor of mathematics.

the-laws-of-thought.name: The Laws of Thought
the-laws-of-thought.summary: George Boole's 1854 book on algebraic logic, introducing what became known as Boolean algebra, foundational to computing.

boolean-algebra.name: Boolean algebra
boolean-algebra.summary: A branch of algebra that works with true and false values using logical operators like and, or and not, introduced by George Boole in 1847 and fundamental to digital electronics.

louis-auguste-blanqui.name: Blanqui
louis-auguste-blanqui.summary: French socialist revolutionary and philosopher (1805–1881) who called for a secretive revolutionary vanguard to seize power and impose a temporary dictatorship on the way to an egalitarian, communist society.

blanquism.name: Blanquism
blanquism.summary: A revolutionary idea tied to Louis-Auguste Blanqui (1805–1881), holding that socialism should be seized by a small, secretive group through a coup rather than a mass uprising.

july-revolution.name: July Revolution
july-revolution.summary: An 1830 uprising in France that overthrew King Charles X and installed his cousin Louis Philippe as a constitutional monarch, ending Bourbon rule in favor of the Orléans branch.

friedrich-engels.name: Friedrich Engels
friedrich-engels.summary: A German philosopher and revolutionary socialist who co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Karl Marx and completed Marx's Das Kapital after his death.

the-condition-of-the-working-class-in-en.name: The Condition of the Working Class in England
the-condition-of-the-working-class-in-en.summary: An 1845 study by Friedrich Engels of the industrial working class in Victorian England, based on his 1842–1844 stay in Manchester and Salford, which deeply impressed Karl Marx.
the-condition-of-the-working-class-in-en.source_title: The Condition of the Working Class in England

salford.name: Salford
salford.summary: A city in Greater Manchester, England, on the River Irwell across from Manchester, whose economy in the 18th and 19th centuries centered on cotton and silk textile mills and an inland port.

karl-marx.name: Karl Marx
karl-marx.summary: German philosopher and revolutionary socialist (1818-1883) who developed historical materialism and co-authored The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels; his ideas, Marxism, greatly influenced political and social history.

immanuel-kant.name: Immanuel Kant
immanuel-kant.summary: German Enlightenment philosopher (1724–1804) whose work on knowledge, ethics and metaphysics, especially the Critique of Pure Reason, made him among the most influential thinkers in Western philosophy.

german-idealism.name: German idealism
german-idealism.summary: A philosophical movement in Germany in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, developed from Kant's work and including Fichte, Schelling and Hegel.

biographia-literaria.name: Biographia Literaria
biographia-literaria.summary: A critical autobiography by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, published in 1817, shaped by William Wordsworth's theory of poetry and Kantian ideas about imagination.

hippolyte-taine.name: Hippolyte Taine
hippolyte-taine.summary: A French historian, critic and philosopher (1828–1893), a chief influence on French naturalism and sociological positivism, whose work shaped writers like Zola and later French right-wing historiography.

victor-cousin.name: Victor Cousin
victor-cousin.summary: A French philosopher (1792–1867) who founded 'eclecticism,' blending German idealism with Scottish Common Sense Realism, and shaped French education policy as administrator of public instruction.

paris-commune.name: Paris Commune
paris-commune.summary: A French revolutionary government that seized control of Paris in March 1871 and governed the city for two months before its defeat.

william-stanley-jevons.name: William Stanley Jevons
william-stanley-jevons.summary: English economist and logician (1835–1882) whose 1871 book helped found the mathematical, marginal-utility approach to economics, alongside similar work by Carl Menger and Léon Walras.

lewis-carroll.name: Lewis Carroll
lewis-carroll.summary: Pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (1832-1898), English author, mathematician and Anglican deacon best known for Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and its wordplay-filled sequel.

what-the-tortoise-said-to-achilles.name: What the Tortoise Said to Achilles
what-the-tortoise-said-to-achilles.summary: An 1895 allegorical dialogue by Lewis Carroll about the foundations of logic, in which a tortoise leads Achilles into an infinite regression of reasoning.
what-the-tortoise-said-to-achilles.source_title: What the Tortoise Said to Achilles

j-m-e-mctaggart.name: J. M. E. McTaggart
j-m-e-mctaggart.summary: English philosopher (1866–1925), a fellow at Trinity College, Cambridge, and one of the leading British idealists influenced by Hegel.

the-unreality-of-time.name: The Unreality of Time
the-unreality-of-time.summary: British philosopher J. M. E. McTaggart's best-known work, first published in 1908, arguing that time is unreal because descriptions of it are contradictory, circular, or insufficient.

b-theory-of-time.name: B-theory of time
b-theory-of-time.summary: A position in the philosophy of time holding that past, present and future are equally real, and that the sense of time flowing is a subjective illusion rather than an objective feature of reality.

pope-pius-vii.name: Pope Pius VII
pope-pius-vii.summary: Head of the Catholic Church from 1800 to 1823, who signed the 1801 Concordat with Napoleon and later excommunicated him after the 1809 invasion of the Papal States.

concordat-of-1801.name: Concordat of 1801
concordat-of-1801.summary: An agreement between Napoleon Bonaparte and Pope Pius VII, signed 15 July 1801, restoring the Catholic Church's civil status in France while giving Napoleon power over bishops and church finances.

charles-frederick-worth.name: Charles Frederick Worth
charles-frederick-worth.summary: English fashion designer (1825–1895) who founded the House of Worth in Paris, considered the father of haute couture and credited with revolutionizing the fashion business.

georges-eug-ne-haussmann.name: Georges-Eugène Haussmann
georges-eug-ne-haussmann.summary: French official (1809-1891) known as Baron Haussmann, who supervised the radical rebuilding of Paris with new boulevards, parks and public works under Napoleon III.

montmartre.name: Montmartre
montmartre.summary: A hill in northern Paris topped by the Sacré-Cœur basilica, famed as an artists' quarter where painters such as Picasso, Monet, and Renoir lived and worked.

highgate-cemetery.name: Highgate Cemetery
highgate-cemetery.summary: A North London burial ground designed by Stephen Geary, holding roughly 170,000 people in about 53,000 graves and also functioning as a de facto nature reserve.

dreyfus-affair.name: Dreyfus affair
dreyfus-affair.summary: A political scandal that divided France from 1894 to 1906 after Captain Alfred Dreyfus was wrongly convicted of treason, splitting the country into Dreyfusard and anti-Dreyfusard camps.

assumptionists.name: Assumptionists
assumptionists.summary: A worldwide Catholic congregation of priests and brothers whose French branch played a major role in 19th-century French political and social history.

pope-leo-xiii.name: Pope Leo XIII
pope-leo-xiii.summary: Head of the Catholic Church from 1878 to 1903, called the "Pope of the Workers" for his 1891 encyclical on workers' rights and known for reviving the philosophy of Thomas Aquinas.

pierre-waldeck-rousseau.name: Pierre Waldeck-Rousseau
pierre-waldeck-rousseau.summary: French Republican politician (1846–1904) who served as Prime Minister of France from 1899 to 1902 while also holding the Interior Ministry.

mile-combes.name: Émile Combes
mile-combes.summary: French politician and freemason (1835–1921) who led the Coalition of the Left cabinet from 1902 to 1905.
